children: The global competition for capital is intensifying, and shifting dynamics in Japan
are creating new pressures for U.S. bond
investors, according to the BlackRock Investment Institute.
Rising domestic yields could potentially "draw some capital home and dent U.S. Treasury demand," strategist Wei Li wrote in a recent note.

However, tightening policy poses distinct domestic risks; with Japan's government debt standing at more than twice its gross domestic product, higher rates make borrowing costly. With markets fully pricing in a Bank of Japan rate hike this month, "fiscal-dominance risk" is coming into sharper focus, the note said.

The implications extend far beyond Japan's borders. Historically, decades of ultra-low domestic yields made Japan a major capital exporter, and the country currently holds some $1.1T in U.S. Treasuries. BlackRock cautioned that even an illustrative 5% shift in these holdings—around $55B—would be "meaningful at the margin." For scale, this shift represents roughly 7% of the Treasury's expected net borrowing for the quarter, highlighting how intensely governments are competing for a finite pool of capital.

The core risk is a global feedback loop: higher U.S. rates could further weaken the yen, pressuring the BoJ to tighten policy faster. On the other hand, higher Japanese rates could repatriate capital, "weakening demand for Treasuries and pushing U.S. borrowing costs higher."

title: Attention U.S. bond investors: Japan’s yield spike could draw capital home
